chapters.name: Chapter 1: Choosing and registering your business

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a business structure
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Pick the business structure that fits your business today, and know what it costs to form.
This lesson builds toward: Given your business idea, owners and risks, you will choose a business structure and list what it costs to form, with one reason for the choice and the fee checked on the Secretary of State page.
Your business structure is the legal form of your business. The most common choices for small businesses are a sole proprietorship, a general partnership, a limited liability company (LLC) and a corporation.
A sole proprietorship is one person doing business. You do not file formation papers with the California Secretary of State, so there is no state formation fee. But you and the business are the same in the eyes of the law: if the business owes money or is sued, your personal things can be at risk. A partnership is the same idea with two or more owners.
An LLC or a corporation is a separate legal body. You form it by filing with the California Secretary of State. The Secretary of State lists the fee for LLC Articles of Organization (Form LLC-1) as $70 and for general stock corporation Articles of Incorporation (Form ARTS-GS) as $100. An LLC or corporation can help protect your personal things from business debts, but it costs more every year (Lesson 6).
There is no single right answer. A one-person cleaning service just starting out may begin as a sole proprietor; a restaurant with a lease, staff and more risk often forms an LLC or corporation. Talk it through with a free SBDC advisor, SCORE mentor or a tax professional before you decide.
Step by step:
- Write down who owns the business and how much risk it carries (lease, staff, customers on site, loans).
- Read the FTB Guide to Common Forms of Ownership.
- Compare the yearly costs, not just the setup fee.
- Choose a structure, and ask an advisor if you are unsure.
Words to know:
- Business structure: the legal form of a business, like sole proprietorship, LLC or corporation.
- Sole proprietorship: a business owned by one person that is not separate from the owner in law.
- LLC: limited liability company: a business registered with the state that is separate from its owners.
- Liability: being legally responsible for a debt or a harm.
Official sources:
- California Secretary of State: Limited Liability Companies (forms and fees)
- California Secretary of State: Corporations (forms and fees)
- Franchise Tax Board: Guide to Common Forms of Ownership (FTB 1123)
Try it now: Start your setup plan. At the top write your business idea, who owns it, and its biggest risks. Then write the structure you would choose today and one reason why.
You can now name the common business structures, say what forming an LLC or corporation costs at the state, and choose one for your business.

check.q: Which structure needs no formation filing with the California Secretary of State?
check.why: A sole proprietorship does not file formation papers with the Secretary of State.

check.q: You want to form an LLC and see a fee online. What would you do before paying?
options: Check the current fee on the Secretary of State's official page
Pay the first website that appears
Ask a friend what they paid years ago
check.why: Fees change, so you check the official page before paying.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Naming and registering your business
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Register your business name the right way for your structure.
This lesson builds toward: Given your business name and structure, you will find how to register your business name, with the right office, its fee page and the publishing rule written in your plan.
An LLC or corporation registers its name when it files its formation papers with the Secretary of State. You can file online at bizfile Online (bizfileonline.sos.ca.gov). Search the name there first to see whether another business already uses it.
If you do business under a name that is not your own legal name, you file a Fictitious Business Name (FBN) statement, also called a DBA ("doing business as"), with the county clerk in the county where your business is based. For example, if Maria Lopez runs "Sunrise Tamales", she files an FBN. An LLC that uses a different name from its registered one files an FBN too.
The fee for an FBN is set by each county, so look it up on your county clerk's website. Counties also require you to publish the FBN in a local newspaper once a week for four weeks, usually starting within 30 days of filing, and then file proof of publication. Check your county's exact rules.
Step by step:
- Search your name idea on bizfile Online.
- LLC or corporation: file the formation papers on bizfile Online.
- Using a name that is not your legal name: file an FBN with your county clerk.
- Publish the FBN in a newspaper as your county requires, and file the proof.
- Write each step, its office and its cost in your plan.
Words to know:
- Fictitious Business Name (FBN): a business name that is not the owner's legal name; also called a DBA.
- DBA: "doing business as": the name a business uses with the public.
- County clerk: the county office that files FBN statements and other public records.
Official sources:
- California Secretary of State: bizfile Online
- Los Angeles County Clerk: Fictitious Business Name requirements (example county)
- California Office of the Small Business Advocate: Set Up Your Business
Try it now: Search your business name on bizfile Online. Then find your county clerk's FBN page and write down the filing fee and the publishing rule in your plan.
You can now check whether a business name is free, and say when you need a Fictitious Business Name and where to file it.

options: The name a business uses with the public, if not the owner's legal name
check.why: A DBA is the public name of a business that differs from the owner's legal name.

check.q: You filed a Fictitious Business Name with your county. What would you most likely do next?
options: Publish it in a local newspaper as your county requires
File it again with the IRS
check.why: Most California counties require you to publish an FBN in a local newspaper.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Getting your free EIN and a seller's permit
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Apply for an EIN from the IRS and decide whether you need a California seller's permit.
This lesson builds toward: Given your business type, you will decide whether you need a seller's permit and list how to get a free EIN, naming the IRS and CDTFA as the offices and using no paid EIN service.
An EIN (Employer Identification Number) is your business's federal tax number. LLCs, corporations, partnerships and any business with employees need one; a sole proprietor without employees may use their own number but often gets an EIN to keep business and personal separate. The IRS says you never have to pay a fee for an EIN. Apply on irs.gov, and beware of websites that charge for it.
A seller's permit comes from the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA). If you sell or lease goods that are normally taxable in California, you need one, and you must display it at your place of business. A shop, a boutique, a food truck and a restaurant usually need one. A pure service, like house cleaning or tutoring, often does not, but check.
CDTFA says there is no fee for a seller's permit, but it may ask for a security deposit, and decides the amount when you apply. If you sell in one place for 90 days or less, such as a seasonal stand, you may need a temporary seller's permit instead. Register online through CDTFA.
Step by step:
- Go to irs.gov and search "apply for an EIN".
- Apply online in one sitting and save the confirmation letter.
- Decide whether you sell taxable goods.
- If yes, register for a seller's permit on cdtfa.ca.gov.
- Display the permit where you do business.
Words to know:
- EIN: Employer Identification Number: a free federal tax number for a business, from the IRS.
- Seller's permit: a California permit, from CDTFA, to sell taxable goods and collect sales tax.
- CDTFA: California Department of Tax and Fee Administration.
- Security deposit: money CDTFA may hold in case sales tax is not paid later.
Official sources:
- IRS: Get an Employer Identification Number
- CDTFA: Permits and Licenses
- CDTFA: Obtaining a Seller's Permit (FAQ)
Try it now: Add two rows to your plan: EIN (IRS, free, apply on irs.gov) and seller's permit (CDTFA, no fee, possible deposit) or a note saying why you do not need one. Do not type your Social Security number anywhere except the official IRS form.
You can now apply for a free EIN on the official IRS site and decide whether your business needs a seller's permit.

check.q: Which agency issues California seller's permits?
check.why: The California Department of Tax and Fee Administration issues seller's permits.

check.q: You plan to sell goods only at a holiday market for a few weeks. What would you do?
options: Ask CDTFA about a temporary seller's permit
Skip permits because it is short
Pay a private site for a permit
check.why: Short-term sellers can ask CDTFA about a temporary seller's permit.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Local permits, yearly costs and your plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding your city and county permits
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use CalGold and your city's website to list the local permits your business needs.
This lesson builds toward: Using CalGold and your city's website, you will list the local permits your business needs, with each agency's website and the fee or where to look it up. Given every step from the course, you will create a one-page setup plan with steps in order, offices, costs and due dates, with every cost checked on the official page or marked "look up at" with where.
Most cities require a business license or business tax certificate, even for a home business. The cost is set by each city (or the county, if you are outside a city) and often depends on your type of business or your income. Look it up on your city's website or call city hall.
Some businesses need special permits. A restaurant or food truck needs a health permit from the county environmental health department. A home bakery may need a cottage food registration or permit from the county. A salon needs state board licenses for the workers. Many places also need a zoning check, a fire inspection or a sign permit.
CalGold (calgold.ca.gov) is a free state tool that helps you find permit information. You choose your city or county and your business type, and it lists the agencies and how to reach them. CalGold does not issue permits, and it says it is still being built, so call the agency to confirm.
Step by step:
- Open calgold.ca.gov.
- Choose your city or county.
- Choose your business type (or "General Business Information").
- Write down each permit and the agency that issues it.
- Visit or call each agency to confirm the fee and how to apply.
Words to know:
- Business license: a city or county permission to run a business there; sometimes called a business tax certificate.
- Zoning: local rules about what kind of business can operate at an address.
- CalGold: a free California website that lists permit information by place and business type.
Official sources:
- CalGold: California permit assistance
- California Office of the Small Business Advocate: Set Up Your Business
Try it now: Run CalGold for your city and business type. Add every permit it lists to your plan, with the agency's website. For each one, write the fee or "look up at" plus where.
You can now find the city and county permits your business needs and the office that issues each one.

options: Lists permit information and agencies for your city and business type
check.why: CalGold lists permits and agencies, but does not issue them.

check.q: CalGold lists a permit for your food truck. What would you do next?
options: Contact the listed agency to confirm the fee and apply
Ask AI to apply for you
check.why: CalGold does not issue permits, so you contact each agency.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The yearly costs: the $800 tax, filings and payroll
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the yearly state costs and deadlines that come with your structure.
This lesson builds toward: Given your structure and hiring plans, you will list the yearly state costs and deadlines, including the $800 tax, the Statement of Information and EDD registration where they apply, each checked on the official page.
LLCs: the Franchise Tax Board (FTB) says every LLC doing business or organized in California must pay an $800 annual tax, every year, until the LLC is cancelled, even if it does no business. The first payment is due by the 15th day of the 4th month after you file with the Secretary of State. LLCs that make more than $250,000 also pay an LLC fee. A first-year exemption that existed for 2021 to 2023 no longer applies.
Corporations: FTB says corporations pay a minimum franchise tax of $800, but newly formed corporations are not required to pay the minimum in their first taxable year. They may still owe tax on income and must make estimated payments.
Statement of Information: LLCs and corporations file one with the Secretary of State. An LLC's Statement of Information (LLC-12) is $20, due within 90 days of forming and every two years after. A stock corporation's (SI-550) is $25. Missing it can bring penalties.
Hiring workers: register with the Employment Development Department (EDD) within 15 days after you pay more than $100 in wages in a quarter. Payroll rules are detailed, so many owners use a payroll service or a tax professional.
Words to know:
- Franchise Tax Board (FTB): California's state tax agency for income and franchise tax.
- Annual tax: the $800 yearly tax every California LLC pays.
- Statement of Information: a short form LLCs and corporations file with the Secretary of State to keep their details current.
- EDD: Employment Development Department: the state office for payroll taxes and employers.
Official sources:
- Franchise Tax Board: Limited liability company
- Franchise Tax Board: Corporations
- California Secretary of State: Limited Liability Companies (forms and fees)
- California Secretary of State: Corporations (forms and fees)
- EDD: Step 1, Register as an Employer
Try it now: Add the yearly rows to your plan that match your structure: the $800 tax and its due date, the Statement of Information and its fee, and EDD registration if you will hire. Open each official page and check the number before you write it.
You can now list the yearly state costs and deadlines for your structure and say which office collects each one.

check.q: How often does an LLC file a Statement of Information after the first one?
check.why: After the first one, an LLC files a Statement of Information every two years.

check.q: Your LLC made no money this year. What would you plan for?
options: Nothing, since there was no business
The $800 annual tax is still owed until the LLC is cancelled
check.why: An LLC owes the $800 annual tax until it is cancelled, even with no business.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Putting it together: your setup plan and budget
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a one-page setup plan with steps in order, offices, costs and due dates.
This lesson builds toward: Given every step from the course, you will create a one-page setup plan with steps in order, offices, costs and due dates, with every cost checked on the official page or marked "look up at" with where.
Now put it all on one page. Order matters: choose a structure, form the LLC or corporation (if any), get the EIN, file the FBN (if needed), get the seller's permit (if needed), then get city and county permits. Many permits ask for your EIN or your entity number, so do those first.
Add up the costs you know, and mark the ones you still need to look up. Example for an LLC food truck: LLC-1 $70, Statement of Information $20, EIN free, seller's permit no fee (deposit possible), $800 annual tax, plus county health permit, city license and FBN fees that you look up locally.
An AI assistant can help you format the table and make a checklist, but it can be wrong about fees and dates. Always use the official page for the number. Do not type your Social Security number, bank details or passwords into an AI tool. When you are done, show the plan to a free SBDC advisor or a tax professional.
Step by step:
- List the steps in order.
- Add the office and official website for each.
- Add the cost from the official page, or "look up at ...".
- Add the due date for each yearly item.
- Total the known costs and show the plan to an advisor.
Words to know:
- Startup costs: the money you spend once to open the business.
- Recurring costs: costs you pay again every year, like the $800 tax.
Official sources:
- California Secretary of State: Limited Liability Companies (forms and fees)
- Franchise Tax Board: Limited liability company
- CDTFA: Permits and Licenses
- IRS: Get an Employer Identification Number
- CalGold: California permit assistance
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page plan with five columns: Step, Office (website), Cost, Due date, Done. Fill in every row from this course, total the known costs, and mark every local fee you still need to look up.
You can now build and use a complete setup plan for starting a business in California.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Structure and name No structure chosen, or the name filing is missing. Structure with a reason, plus the right name filing and its office. Also notes the FBN publishing rule if it applies. EIN and seller's permit Missing, or uses a paid EIN service. EIN from irs.gov at no cost, and a seller's permit row or a reason it is not needed. Notes a possible CDTFA security deposit. Local permits No city license or CalGold permits listed. City business license and every CalGold permit, each with the agency's website. Each local fee is filled in from the official page. Yearly costs and due dates The $800 tax or Statement of Information is missing for an LLC or corporation. Yearly rows that match the structure, with due dates. Includes EDD registration if hiring, and each number checked on the official page. Plan in order with costs Steps out of order, or costs guessed. Five columns filled in order, with known costs totaled and unknown fees marked "look up at". Every official website is listed and the Done column is in use. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: In what order should you usually do these steps?
options: Choose a structure, form it, get the EIN, then local permits
Local permits, then choose a structure
Get the EIN before choosing a name or structure, then form it last
check.why: Each step depends on the one before it, starting with the structure.

check.q: You do not know your city's business license fee yet. What would you write in your plan?
options: "Look up at" plus the city's official website
check.why: Local fees differ, so you note where to look them up instead of guessing.
